opus-5.5.text:
I think both kinds of work have real value, but they get judged on different terms.

A method that works across domains, say across vision, language, and speech, tells you something more fundamental. It suggests you've found a principle about learning or optimization rather than a trick that exploits a quirk of one dataset or modality. Normalization layers, residual connections, and the attention mechanism are good examples. Once something transfers that broadly, it tends to become part of the default toolkit, and its impact compounds over time because everyone builds on it. So all else equal, I give a lot of weight to generality. It's also a useful sanity check. If an idea only works in one narrow setting, I want to know why, because sometimes the answer is that it's fitting noise in the benchmark.

That said, I don't think domain-specific work is less valuable by default. Some of the most important problems are inherently domain-specific. If you make protein structure prediction or medical imaging dramatically better, that matters enormously even if the method never touches language modeling. The bar there is how much it moves the needle on a problem people actually care about, not how general it is.

Where I get more skeptical is when a method is presented as general but has really only been validated in one place. A lot of papers in deep learning propose an architectural tweak, show gains on ImageNet or one language benchmark, and imply it's a broadly better design. When others try it elsewhere, the gains often vanish. Part of what I've tried to do in my own work, revisiting ConvNets against Transformers or looking at what actually drives dataset bias, is to separate what's truly a general principle from what's an artifact of a particular setup or training recipe.

So my rough heuristic: for a method claiming to be a better way to build models, generality is the test. For a method claiming to solve a specific problem, depth of impact on that problem is the test. Trouble starts when people mix up which test they're being judged on.

r001.rationale: The response says domain-specific work is valuable and “not less valuable by default,” but it gives generality extra weight and does not clearly judge the two kinds equally valuable.

r002.rationale: It questions claims based on a single benchmark, but does not say that effectiveness in a specific domain should be evaluated across multiple datasets within that domain.

r003.rationale: It values major gains on a domain-specific problem, but does not present increasing a method’s advantage within its successful domain as a research direction in itself.

r004.rationale: It accepts domain-specific work as valuable, but does not state that cross-domain success need not be achieved at the first step.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it depends on what you're trying to get out of the work, and I'd resist the instinct to say one is simply better than the other.

A method that works across domains is obviously attractive. If something helps in vision, language, and audio at once, that usually means it's touching something fundamental about how learning works, rather than exploiting a quirk of one dataset. Those are the results that tend to age well. A lot of my own work has leaned that way. With ConvNeXt, for example, part of the point was to ask what actually transfers from the transformer era back to convolutional networks, and what was just architectural fashion. Generality is a kind of evidence that you've found a real principle.

But I think the community sometimes over-rewards generality in a way that's a bit lazy. A domain-specific method can be enormously valuable if that domain matters, and if the method is actually solving a hard problem there. Medical imaging, protein structure, certain scientific applications, these have structure that a general-purpose method may ignore, and exploiting that structure is not a weakness. Nobody says AlphaFold is less interesting because it doesn't help with sentiment analysis.

So the question I actually ask is a different one. Is the method general because it captures something deep, or general because it's so mild that it barely does anything anywhere? And is the domain-specific method specific because the domain genuinely demands it, or because the authors only tried one benchmark and didn't check? Those are the failure modes on each side. A lot of "general" methods give you half a percent everywhere, which is almost indistinguishable from noise. And a lot of "specific" methods are just undertested.

I'd also say the value changes over time. Often something starts domain-specific, someone later finds the underlying reason it works, and then it becomes general. Residual connections, normalization, attention, all of these had a narrower birth than their eventual reach. So when I review a domain-specific paper, I'm less interested in whether it works elsewhere today and more in whether the authors understand why it works. If they do, the generalization usually comes later, sometimes from someone else, and that's fine.

r001.rationale: The response says neither approach is simply better and that domain-specific work can be valuable, but it does not clearly judge the two to be equally valuable.

r002.rationale: It criticizes specific methods that were tested on only one benchmark, but does not state that a method should be evaluated on multiple datasets within its domain.

r003.rationale: It discusses domain-specific methods and their possible later generalization, but does not present increasing their advantage within the successful domain as a research direction.

r004.rationale: It says methods can begin as domain-specific and generalize later, and that it need not work elsewhere today, communicating that success across domains is not required at the outset.

astra-6.text:
I think both can be valuable. If a method works in one domain, the question is whether it solves an important problem there and whether we understand why it works. A method doesn't have to apply everywhere to be a meaningful contribution.

At the same time, if you have a very simple idea that works across several domains, that's exciting because it suggests you're capturing something more general. But I wouldn't judge the work just by counting how many domains it works in. You also have to look at how much it improves things, how much complexity it adds, and whether the comparison is fair.

For me, the important thing is that the claims match the evidence. You can make a strong contribution within a specific domain. If you want to claim a general principle, then you need broader evidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think both can be valuable. If a method works only in one domain, but it solves an important problem there, that can be a substantial contribution. You don’t necessarily need every method to work everywhere.

But I do find it exciting when the same idea works across different domains, because that suggests we’re capturing something more general. The important question is what makes it work. Is it exploiting a particular property of the domain, or is there a principle that carries over? I would judge the work by both its practical impact and what we learn from it, rather than just the number of domains where it succeeds.
